final_recommendation: The room converged on a Protocol amendment with automatic tariff suspension on verified labor violations, three-person panel with Mexican chair and two-of-three majority rule, scope locked to labor enforcement only. Congress commits to March vote contingent on Thursday draft delivery; business lobby secures immediate announcement to lock momentum.
minority_objections: Labor union initially demanded independent inspectors with no Mexican veto, resisted joint teams until automatic trigger was locked
Canada repeatedly insisted on explicit scope limits to prevent reopening dairy/Chapter 19, threatened to walk if amendment expanded beyond labor
key_conflicts: Mexico sovereignty vs. U.S. enforcement credibility: resolved via Mexican-chaired panel with binding majority rule
Announcement timing: Congress/labor demanded Thursday draft before March vote announcement; business lobby pushed immediate announcement for momentum
Automatic trigger definition: Congress required same-day tariff suspension on panel finding, no cure period or written-award delay
key_concessions: Mexico accepted automatic tariff suspension and binding panel majority rule in exchange for Mexican chair and scope limits
Congress accepted Mexican-chaired panel in exchange for two-of-three majority rule and no cure period
Canada accepted labor amendment in exchange for explicit scope lock preventing reopening of dairy/Chapter 19/rules of origin
Labor union accepted joint inspection teams (Mexican lead) in exchange for automatic trigger and written violation definitions
red_lines: Congress: no March vote without Thursday draft showing automatic trigger and two-of-three panel rule in writing
Mexico: no U.S. unilateral enforcement; panel must have Mexican chair and binding arbitration
Canada: amendment scope locked to labor only; dairy/Chapter 19/rules of origin not subject to reopening
Labor union: no public endorsement without seeing arbitration text Thursday night; no cure period or enforcement delays
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Implementation risk: no discussion of how joint inspection teams would actually operate on the ground or resource requirements
Timeline feasibility: Thursday EOD draft deadline extremely tight; no contingency if legal drafting slips
Political fragility: 80-vote commitment contingent on perfect draft execution; no buffer for technical ambiguities
Canadian domestic backlash: scope-lock language may not be sufficient to defend dairy concession politically if opposition frames amendment as precedent for reopening
downstream_risk_variables: Thursday draft quality and clarity on 'automatic' and 'credible finding' definitions
Media narrative Friday morning: whether draft is framed as 'locked mechanism' or 'ambiguous language'
Labor union membership reaction to joint teams with Mexican lead inspectors
Canadian opposition's ability to exploit amendment as precedent for future renegotiation
Mexico's domestic political capacity to defend automatic tariff suspension as sovereignty-respecting
uncertainty_notes: Room locked technical commitments but did not stress-test implementation: how joint teams resolve inspection disputes in real time, whether two-of-three majority rule prevents panel deadlock, whether Thursday draft can actually capture all verbal commitments without ambiguity. Announcement-before-draft sequence (business lobby's win) creates narrative risk if draft shows gaps. Canada's scope-lock language may not survive domestic political scrutiny if framed as opening door to future amendments.

marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Congress's 80-vote commitment contingent on Thursday draft drove every round; 'my votes don't hold' and 'votes crater in 48 hours' repeated throughout as central constraint
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_pressure: Automatic tariff suspension, no cure period, two-of-three panel rule dominated all five rounds; labor union's 'I don't endorse until I see text' set the enforcement floor
marker_evidence.business_lobby_support: Business lobby pushed March announcement for certainty but was secondary to enforcement mechanics; 'lock in market certainty' mentioned but not driving the technical negotiations
marker_evidence.canadian_domestic_acceptability: Canada's dairy/Chapter 19 scope lock was a recurring red line ('we're out' if amendment expands) but not the room's dominant thread; resolved via explicit scope language
marker_evidence.mexico_labor_sovereignty_risk: Mexican chair, binding arbitration, joint teams with Mexican lead drove Mexico's participation; 'U.S. agents in Mexican factories' and sovereignty language central to Mexico's position throughout
marker_evidence.media_public_pressure: Media actor framed headlines as credibility test ('enforcement locked' vs 'ambiguous language') but was reactive to technical commitments, not driving them
marker_evidence.agreement_stability: Room treated amendment as necessary for ratification ('the whole deal collapses' if Mexico walks, 'momentum dies' without announcement) but stability was contingent on technical execution, not the dominant analytical frame

node: Node 2 - Domestic Ratification Pressure Room (initial USMCA package formed, before the 10 Dec 2019 Protocol of Amendment; information cutoff 2019-12-09)
